summary: Give the Pizza size calculator the price, the true cost and the crust and it returns edible area (Smaller pizza extra info). That makes it useful for portioning, timing or nutrition. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Pizza size calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pizza size calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports edible area (Smaller pizza extra info) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the price (Smaller pizza), the true cost (Smaller pizza), the crust (Smaller pizza extra info) and the toppings (Smaller pizza extra info).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Price (Smaller pizza): a measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.
  • True cost (Smaller pizza): a measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.
  • Crust (Smaller pizza extra info): a measured quantity, entered by default in square centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • Toppings (Smaller pizza extra info): a measured quantity, entered by default in square centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • True cost (Larger pizza): a measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.
  • Edible area (Larger pizza extra info): a measured quantity, entered by default in square centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pizza size calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Edible area=price ÷ true cost
Do you eat the crust?=the square root of (edible area) ÷ (the square root of (PI) × crust size) + (1 ÷ 2) × diameter ÷ crust size
Price=edible area × true cost
Diameter=2 × the square root of (edible area) ÷ the square root of (PI) + 2 × crust size × do you eat the crust?
Crust size=(1 ÷ 2) × diameter + (1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (-4 × crust + PI × (diameter ^ 2)) ÷ the square root of (PI)
Diameter=2 × the square root of (crust + toppings) ÷ the square root of (PI)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.html:

  • Price (Larger pizza): shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.
  • Diameter (Larger pizza): shown in centimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Crust size: shown in centimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Diameter (Smaller pizza): shown in centimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Crust (Larger pizza extra info): shown in square centimeters, and convertible to any of the 24 units on that chip.
  • Toppings (Larger pizza extra info): shown in square centimeters, and convertible to any of the 24 units on that chip.
  • Toppings cover (Smaller pizza): a number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Toppings cover (Larger pizza): a number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Crust size: Length, opening in centimeters
  • Diameter (Smaller pizza): Length, opening in centimeters
  • Price (Smaller pizza): Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • True cost (Smaller pizza): Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Edible area (Smaller pizza extra info): Area, opening in square centimeters
  • Crust (Smaller pizza extra info): Area, opening in square centimeters
  • Toppings (Smaller pizza extra info): Area, opening in square centimeters
  • Diameter (Larger pizza): Length, opening in centimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pizza size calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Scaling a recipe up or down
  • Working out timing so everything finishes together
  • Checking portions before you shop
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the price, the true cost and the crust — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pizza size calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns edible area (Smaller pizza extra info), derived from the price, the true cost and the crust. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pizza size calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the price, the true cost and the crust, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter crust size in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Crust size opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Pizza size calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
